q914: Orienting is one of the oldest responses in the nervous system. Deep in the brainstem, a region that controls eye and head movements is constantly checking the surroundings for danger. When you are anxious, your eyes often lock onto one spot or dart around tensely, which keeps the alarm switched on. Turning the head and eyes slowly lets this system complete its scan and report that nothing is wrong. Noticing exits, light and open space answers the survival brain's basic questions, can I get out, can I see. Resting your gaze on something pleasant adds a small signal of comfort. Many people feel a deep breath or a softening in the belly within a minute. Repeated often, this teaches your body to trust safe places more readily.
q915: God made our bodies to be watchful because He cares about our protection. A sheep looks around before it settles to graze, and a child glances back to see that a parent is still there. This watchfulness is not a flaw, but it needs a way to switch off. God built that switch into the simple act of looking and finding safety. It shows a Creator who wants us to rest, not live braced for attack. It also reminds us that our nervous system is designed to learn from what it actually sees, not only from what it fears. As you practise orienting, you are cooperating with that design. Over time you become more able to rest in God's care, seeing your surroundings and your life with calmer, clearer eyes.
q916: The Bible takes overwhelm seriously. David prayed, "From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I" (Psalm 61:2). When the prophet Elijah collapsed in despair, God did not lecture him. He sent an angel who touched him, gave him food and water, and let him sleep before speaking to him (1 Kings 19:5-8). Paul admits being "troubled on every side, yet not distressed" (2 Corinthians 4:8). These passages show that God cares for the whole person, body included, in moments of crisis. Using cool water, movement and breath when emotion is extreme is like Elijah's bread and water, practical help that steadies the body so the heart can hear God again.
q917: When emotion climbs above seven out of ten, the thinking brain struggles to work, so talking yourself down rarely helps. TIPP works through the body instead. Cool water on the face and around the eyes triggers the dive reflex through the facial nerves, and the vagus nerve slows the heart within seconds. Intense exercise uses up the adrenaline and stress energy your body has released, finishing the stress response rather than leaving it stuck. Paced breathing, with a longer out-breath, keeps the calming branch active. Paired muscle relaxation links breathing out with letting muscles go, and over repeated practice the body learns to relax more easily when you exhale. If you have a heart condition or eating disorder, check with a doctor before using cold water or hard exercise.
q918: God gave our bodies emergency brakes because He knew life in a broken world would sometimes overwhelm us. The dive reflex, the release that follows exercise and the calm of a slow breath are all parts of a design that can bring us back from the edge. This reflects His mercy. He does not expect us to reason our way out of a flood. He made a way that works even when thoughts are scrambled. Using these tools is good stewardship of the body He entrusted to you, not a lack of faith. Once the storm has settled, you can pray, think clearly and make wise choices again. In this way, caring for your body in crisis opens the door to deeper healing of heart and mind.
q919: From the beginning God gave people the work of naming. In Genesis 2:19 Adam named every living creature, bringing order and understanding to the world. The Psalms carry this naming into the inner life. David spoke to his own soul, "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me?" (Psalm 42:5). Psalm 62:8 invites us to pour out our hearts before God, and Jesus Himself wept openly at the grave of His friend (John 11:35). Scripture never asks us to hide or deny our emotions. It shows us how to name them honestly before a God who already knows them. When you say, I feel disappointed and embarrassed, you are doing what the Psalmists did, bringing the truth of your heart into His light.
q920: Research suggests that simply putting a feeling into words calms the brain. In brain scan studies, naming an emotion increased activity in a part of the prefrontal cortex and reduced activity in the amygdala, the brain's alarm centre. Finding where the feeling sits in your body, perhaps a tight throat or heavy chest, uses the insula, which reads body signals and helps you notice emotions earlier. Being specific matters. People who can tell the difference between being annoyed, hurt and lonely tend to handle stress better than those who only say bad. Rating it from zero to ten gives the thinking brain a sense of size, and asking what the feeling needs moves you toward a helpful response. Over weeks, this habit builds a richer and calmer emotional vocabulary.
q921: God made emotions as messengers, not enemies. Fear warns of danger, sadness marks loss, and anger notices injustice. When we ignore them, they often grow louder or come out sideways in our bodies and relationships. By designing the brain so that naming brings calm, God has shown that honesty is a pathway to peace. This reflects His own character. He is truthful, and He invites relationship based on truth, not pretending. When you name what you feel, you also make it possible for others, and for God, to meet you there. A feeling named can be comforted, prayed over and understood. Over time this practice helps you become a whole person whose inner life and outer life match, free to love without hiding.
q922: Paul describes a spiritual battle fought in the mind, "casting down imaginations ... and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5). This assumes something freeing, that you are not the same as every thought in your head. When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He heard the tempter's suggestions without obeying them, answering each with "It is written" (Matthew 4:4). Proverbs 4:23 tells us to keep the heart with all diligence, and Philippians 4:8 directs our attention to what is true and lovely. Cognitive defusion follows this pattern. Instead of believing a thought like I'm useless the moment it appears, you step back and notice it as a thought. Then you can hold it up to the light of God's truth.
q923: Our minds produce thousands of thoughts a day, and many are automatic, shaped by past hurts and habits. When we are fused with a thought, the brain treats it like a fact, and the emotional centres react as if it were true. Saying I'm having the thought that I'm useless adds a layer of awareness. Research suggests this kind of noticing engages regions in the prefrontal cortex involved in observing your own mind, and it reduces how believable and upsetting the thought feels, even though the words have not changed. Naming the story, such as the Not-Good-Enough story, helps you recognise a familiar pattern. Returning attention to your task weakens the habit of rumination. Repeated over weeks, the thought may still come, but it loses much of its power.
q924: God gave us minds capable of watching themselves, something unique among His creatures. That ability exists so that we can choose what to believe and follow, rather than being pushed around by every passing impulse. This reflects the dignity He has given us as people made in His image. It also reflects grace. Defusion does not require you to win an argument with every harsh thought or feel shame for having it. Thoughts arise in a fallen world, and having one is not the same as agreeing with it. God invites you to notice, step back and turn toward His voice. Over time, as you practise this, the voice of accusation grows quieter and the voice of the Shepherd becomes easier to recognise and follow.
q925: The Bible is honest that temptation and craving are part of human life. Jesus Himself was tempted in every way we are, yet without sin, which is why we can come boldly to His throne for help (Hebrews 4:15-16). Paul promises, "God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able" (1 Corinthians 10:13), and he lists self-control as fruit the Spirit grows (Galatians 5:22-23). Psalm 27:14 calls us to wait on the LORD and be of good courage. Urge surfing joins these truths. You do not need to fight in panic or give in. You can wait with God through the wave, watching it rise and fall, trusting that His faithfulness is bigger than the urge and that a way through is already provided.
q926: An urge is a strong signal from the brain's reward system, often driven by dopamine, which rises when we expect relief or pleasure. Each time we act on the urge, the loop of cue, craving and action grows stronger. When you notice the urge, rate it and locate it in your body, you engage awareness networks such as the insula and prefrontal cortex, which helps you watch the craving rather than obey it. Most urges rise, peak and fade within twenty to thirty minutes. Every time one passes without being fed, the brain learns something new, that the urge is survivable and does not need action. This is called extinction learning. Over weeks, urges often come less often and with less force, and you can become curious about what they are really asking for.
q927: God made us with deep desires for comfort, connection and rest. Many unwanted urges are those good longings looking for relief in the wrong place, often when we feel lonely, tired or ashamed. Urge surfing allows you to meet these longings with curiosity rather than contempt. Instead of hating yourself, you can ask what the urge is pointing to and bring that need to God and safe people. This reflects His patient grace. He does not crush the weak but strengthens them. He also designed the brain to change through practice, so freedom grows step by step, not in one moment of willpower. Each wave you ride with Him is a small victory that reshapes your heart and body toward the freedom He longs for you to enjoy.
q928: Scripture often praises the wisdom of pausing before acting. James writes, "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (James 1:19), and Proverbs 16:32 says that he who rules his spirit is greater than one who takes a city. Psalm 4:4 counsels, "Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still." When Nehemiah was asked a sudden, risky question by the king, he first "prayed to the God of heaven" before answering (Nehemiah 2:4). The STOP skill follows this pattern. A brief stop, a breath and a look inside make room for a quick prayer and a wiser response, so that your actions come from your values and not only from your first reaction.
q929: When something triggers you, the alarm centre in the brain reacts within a fraction of a second, much faster than the thinking parts can respond. Stress chemicals like adrenaline rise, the heart speeds up and the body prepares to fight, flee or freeze. Simply freezing for a moment stops the automatic reaction from running all the way. A deep breath sends calming signals through the vagus nerve. Observing what is happening inside and around you engages the prefrontal cortex, which can weigh choices and consider consequences. Asking what action fits your values links the moment to your deeper goals. The more often you use STOP, the more the pause becomes a habit wired into the brain, so that in time it happens almost automatically when pressure rises.
q930: God gave us both quick reactions and slower reflection, and both are good. The fast response protects us from danger, like stepping back from a speeding car. The slower one lets us love, forgive and choose wisely. Sin and stress can make us live only from the fast system, hurting others and ourselves. By designing a pause that lets the wiser parts of the mind catch up, God offers a space where His Spirit can guide us. This reflects His own character. He is slow to anger and abounding in mercy, never rash or cruel. As you practise STOP, you are being shaped into His likeness, becoming a person whose words and actions bring peace, and whose relationships grow safer and kinder over time.
q931: The Bible describes God as deeply compassionate toward our weakness. "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame, he remembereth that we are dust" (Psalm 103:13-14). Lamentations 3:22 says His compassions do not fail, and Hebrews 4:15 tells us Jesus is touched with the feeling of our infirmities. Jesus also commanded us to love our neighbour as ourselves (Mark 12:31), which assumes a healthy, humble care for our own souls. A self-compassion break follows this pattern. You admit the moment is hard, remember that others struggle too, and speak kindly to yourself, echoing the way God speaks to His children. It is not excusing sin. It is receiving His mercy so you can rise again.
q932: When we fail, many of us react with harsh self-criticism. Research suggests this activates the threat system in the brain, increasing stress hormones such as cortisol and making us more anxious and less able to learn from mistakes. Self-compassion engages a different system, linked with care and soothing, involving hormones such as oxytocin and the calming branch of the nervous system. Placing a hand on your heart is a simple form of warm touch that can lower stress responses. Reminding yourself that struggle is part of being human reduces the shame that makes us feel alone. In studies, people who practise self-compassion tend to recover from setbacks faster, take more responsibility and are more willing to try again. Repeated over weeks, this new response becomes easier and more natural.
